title: What might have been
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: LATIN HAS A REAL PAST COUNTERFACTUAL AND THIS MODULE WRITES IT IN FULL: sī vēnissēs, vīdissēs — 'if you had come, you would have seen', the PLUPERFECT SUBJUNCTIVE in both halves. One shape in Latin, two in English: vēnissēs is 'had come' and vīdissēs is 'would have seen', and they are identical, because the MOOD carries 'this did not happen' and the TENSE carries 'before now'. Nothing else is needed. L3-M4 opened the present subjunctive and said the tense a real counterfactual needs was L4's; this is that module.

BOTH HALVES MOVE TOGETHER, AND IN THE PAST THE MIXTURE IS WORSE THAN IN THE PRESENT. L3-M4 spent three plates on mixing an open condition with an imagined one; here a mixed pair has one half ASSERTING that something happened and the other saying it did not, which is not a sentence about anything. Every plate in this module that is not about a negative is about this.

utinam IS A PARTICLE WHOSE ONLY JOB IS TO MARK A WISH, and with the pluperfect subjunctive the wish is about something already settled — which is what a regret IS. utinam vēnissem, 'if only I had come': two words, where English needs three and a tense shift. A negative wish takes nōn, because utinam is not itself a negative. vellem is the other way in — L2-M1's velim one tense back, so velim is a wish still open and vellem one that is closed.

THE IMPERFECT SUBJUNCTIVE IS THE SECOND NEW TENSE AND IT DENIES THE PRESENT: sī venīrēs, gaudērem, 'if you were coming, I should be glad' — you are not coming. Against sī vēnissēs, vīdissēs, which denies the past. One mood, two tenses, and the difference is which time is being denied. This is the shape a learner will need most often, because most of what anyone imagines is about now.

velim WAS THIS MOOD ALL ALONG, AND SO WAS sīs. L2-M1 taught velim as a fixed form and L3-M4 explained sīs; vellem is velim's imperfect subjunctive, and the pair works exactly like S03 against S01 — velim is a wish about something still open and vellem about something closed. Twenty modules of using a word before learning what it was, which is the third time this course has done that deliberately.

nisi IS 'IF NOT' IN ONE WORD, and it is the fourth place in this course where a negative lives inside a word rather than beside one — after L1-M3's nōlō, L2-M9's mālō and L3-M5's negō. sī nōn exists and is clumsier. Adding nōn to nisi gives two negatives that cancel, which is L3-M5's negat sē nōn venīre error on a different word — and utinam, which is NOT a negative, takes nōn and needs it.

THE IMPERFECT SUBJUNCTIVE IS A MOOD AND NOT A TENSE OF THE INDICATIVE. venīrem is 'if I were coming' and the tense that says 'I used to come' is a different word entirely — legēbam, habēbam and eram are STILL free keys after thirty-two modules, and M8 of this level spends them. An author who writes an indicative imperfect here has taken M8's arrival away from it.

sentences.cue: If you had come, you would have seen.

words.note: 'If'. L3-M4's word, and the mood after it decides everything: indicative for an open condition, subjunctive for one merely imagined.
'If you had come' — the pluperfect subjunctive of veniō. It says the coming did NOT happen, which no tense of the indicative can do.
'You would have seen' — the pluperfect subjunctive of videō. Both halves of a past counterfactual take it, and English needs 'had' in one half and 'would have' in the other.

sentences.trap: One tense in Latin, two in English. vēnissēs is 'had come' and vīdissēs is 'would have seen', and they are the SAME shape — the mood carries 'did not happen' and the tense carries 'before now', so nothing else is needed. L3-M4 opened the present subjunctive and said this tense was L4's; here it is.
sentences.sound: SĪ vē-nis-SĒS, vī-dis-SĒS. The two halves rhyme exactly, which is what a counterfactual sounds like.

variations.cue: If I had come, I would have seen.
variations.changed: about the speaker, so both verbs move together

variations.cue: If he had come, he would have seen.
If you had not come, you would not have seen.

mistake.why: one half in the plain perfect. A counterfactual needs both halves imagined — L3-M4 spent three plates on that rule in the present, and in the past the mixture is worse, because the indicative half asserts that the thing DID happen and the other half says it did not.

sentences.mnemonic: Both halves the same shape, and both mean 'did not'.

words.note: 'If only' — a particle for a wish, and with the pluperfect subjunctive it is a wish about the past, which is to say a regret.
'I had come' as an imagined thing — the PLUPERFECT SUBJUNCTIVE. Not a tense you assert with: it exists to say what did not happen.

sentences.trap: Two words and a whole regret. utinam is a particle whose only job is to mark a wish, and with the pluperfect subjunctive the wish is about something already settled — which is what a regret IS. Latin has one word for the job and English has three.
sentences.sound: U-ti-nam vē-NIS-sem. Five syllables, one long vowel, and the stress is on the thing that did not happen.

variations.cue: If only you had come.
If only I had not made a mistake.
variations.changed: L2-M8's verb, and the regret negative

variations.cue: If only I had seen.

mistake.why: the plain perfect after utinam. vēnī asserts that the coming happened, which makes the sentence 'if only I came' with the wish granted — and the whole point of utinam is that it is not.

sentences.mnemonic: utinam plus 'had': a regret in two words.

sentences.cue: If you were coming, I should be glad.

words.note: 'If'. L3-M4's word, and the mood after it decides everything: indicative for an open condition, subjunctive for one merely imagined.
'If you were coming' — the IMPERFECT subjunctive of veniō, denying the present. L3-M4's veniās is the present subjunctive and imagines the future instead.
'I should be glad' — the imperfect subjunctive of L3-M4's gaudeō. Both halves of a present unreal condition take this tense.

sentences.trap: The second new tense of the module, and it is for NOW. sī venīrēs, gaudērem imagines the present — you are not coming, and if you were I should be glad — where sī vēnissēs, vīdissēs imagines the past. One mood, two tenses, and the difference is which time is being denied.
sentences.sound: SĪ ve-NĪ-rēs, gau-DĒ-rem. The long ē of each ending is the mood, and both halves carry one.

variations.cue: If he were coming, I should be glad.
If you were not coming, I should not be glad.
If you were to come, I should be glad.
variations.changed: L3-M4's present subjunctive, which imagines the future rather than denying the present

mistake.why: the second half left in the plain present. Both halves must be imagined, and this is L3-M4's central error on the new tense — the pull is stronger here because gaudeō is the sentence a learner has written since that module.

sentences.usage: Said about something you know is not happening.

words.note: 'I wish' — L2-M1's velim one tense back. That module taught velim as a fixed form; this is its imperfect subjunctive, and it means a wish you know will not be granted.
'I had come' as an imagined thing — the PLUPERFECT SUBJUNCTIVE. Not a tense you assert with: it exists to say what did not happen.

sentences.trap: velim has been in your mouth since L2-M1 and this is what it was all along. velim is 'I should like' about something still open; vellem is 'I wish' about something closed — and the difference between them is the same difference as between S03's tense and S01's.
sentences.sound: VEL-lem vē-NIS-sem. The double l is held and the long ē of vēnissem carries the past.

variations.cue: I wish I had seen.
I wish I had not made a mistake.
I should like you to come.
variations.changed: L2-M1's velim with L3-M4's present subjunctive, which is still open

mistake.why: velim where vellem belongs. velim wishes for something still open and this wish is closed — the coming did not happen — so the present subjunctive contradicts the pluperfect two words later.

sentences.mnemonic: velim is open; vellem is closed.

sentences.cue: If I had not made a mistake, I would have come.

words.note: 'If not, unless' — one word for two, and the fourth place in this course where a negative lives inside a word: nōlō, mālō, negō, nisi.
'If I had not gone wrong' — the pluperfect subjunctive of L2-M8's errō, and the negative is in nisi rather than on the verb.
'I had come' as an imagined thing — the PLUPERFECT SUBJUNCTIVE. Not a tense you assert with: it exists to say what did not happen.

sentences.trap: There is no nōn in this sentence. nisi is 'if not' in one word, and this course has now met four words with a negative inside them — nōlō, mālō, negō and nisi. sī nōn exists and nisi is what a Roman wrote.
sentences.sound: NI-si er-rā-VIS-sem, vē-NIS-sem. Both verbs end on the same two syllables, which is the mood rhyming with itself.

variations.cue: If you had not made a mistake, you would have come.
If I had not been ill, I would have come.
variations.changed: L3-M7's adjective with sum's pluperfect subjunctive

variations.cue: If I had not made a mistake, I would have come.
variations.changed: sī nōn written out, which is correct and clumsier

mistake.why: nōn added to a word that already contains one. This says 'if I had not not made a mistake' — two negatives cancelling, exactly as they did in L3-M5's negat sē nōn venīre, which is the same error on a different word.

sentences.usage: Said blaming yourself for an absence.

sentences.cue: If only I had not made a mistake; I am ashamed.

words.note: 'If only' — a particle for a wish, and with the pluperfect subjunctive it is a wish about the past, which is to say a regret.
'Not', in front of what it denies. After utinam a negative wish takes nōn, because utinam is not a negative itself — nisi is.
'I had gone wrong' — the pluperfect subjunctive of errō.
'Me' — the accusative, because pudet wants it. L3-M6's row.
'It shames' — impersonal, accusative of the person. L3-M6's verb.

sentences.trap: utinam takes nōn and nisi does not, which is the distinction the sentence before this one sets up. utinam is a wish particle with no negative in it, so a negative wish needs one; nisi already has one and refuses a second.
sentences.sound: U-ti-nam nōn er-rā-VIS-sem; MĒ PU-det. Twelve syllables, and the regret is nine of them.

variations.cue: If only you had not made a mistake.
variations.changed: about the listener, and no consequence

variations.cue: If only I had come; I am ashamed.

variations.display: Utinam nōn errāvissem; nōn tamen mē pudet.
variations.cue: If only I had not made a mistake; I am not ashamed, though.
variations.changed: L3-M3's tamen, still second in its clause

mistake.why: nisi used as a wish particle. nisi means 'if not' and opens a condition, so this is half a sentence with no result — utinam is the word for a wish, and it is the only one.

sentences.usage: Said regretting something and feeling it.
sentences.mnemonic: utinam takes nōn; nisi contains it.

sentences.display: Sī hōrā prīmā vēnissēs, medicum vīdissēs.
sentences.cue: If you had come at the first hour, you would have seen the doctor.
sentences.literal: if at-hour first you-had-come doctor you-would-have-seen

words.note: 'If'. L3-M4's word, and the mood after it decides everything: indicative for an open condition, subjunctive for one merely imagined.
'At the hour' — L3-M1's ablative, and the ending is the 'at'.
'First', the ordinal agreeing with hōrā. Not L2-M10's prīmum, which is the adverb.
'If you had come' — the pluperfect subjunctive of veniō.
'Doctor' as the object. L3-M7's word.
'You would have seen' — the pluperfect subjunctive of videō.

sentences.trap: A full counterfactual with a time and an object in it, and nothing in the frame has changed. Both verbs are the same shape, both halves are imagined, and everything between them is L3's — which is what makes one module enough for two new tenses.
sentences.sound: SĪ HŌ-rā PRĪ-mā vē-nis-SĒS, ME-di-cum vī-dis-SĒS. Sixteen syllables, and the two -issēs endings close each half.

variations.display: Sī hōrā sextā vēnissēs, medicum vīdissēs.
variations.cue: If you had come at the sixth hour, you would have seen the doctor.

variations.display: Sī hōrā prīmā vēnissem, medicum vīdissem.
variations.cue: If I had come at the first hour, I would have seen the doctor.

variations.display: Sī hōrā prīmā vēnissēs, mē vīdissēs.
variations.cue: If you had come at the first hour, you would have seen me.

mistake.display: Sī hōrā prīmā vēnissēs, medicum vīdistī.
mistake.why: the second half in the plain perfect. It asserts you did see the doctor, which the first half has just denied — and the longer the sentence, the easier it is to finish it in the tense you would use for a fact.

sentences.mnemonic: Two halves, one mood, however long the line.

sentences.cue: If I were learning the language, I should be reading the books.

words.note: 'If'. L3-M4's word, and the mood after it decides everything: indicative for an open condition, subjunctive for one merely imagined.
'Language' as the thing learned. L3-M2's word.
'If I were learning' — the imperfect subjunctive of discō. It denies the present: I am not learning it.
'Books' as the object — liber, librum, librī, librōs. L1-M4's word.
'I should be reading' — the imperfect subjunctive of legō. Both halves of a present unreal take it.

sentences.trap: Both halves in the imperfect subjunctive, and it denies the present twice. This is the shape a learner will want most often, because most of what we imagine is about now rather than about a particular afternoon — and it is the shape English marks with 'were' and 'should'.
sentences.sound: SĪ LIN-guam dis-CE-rem, LI-brōs LE-ge-rem. Fourteen syllables, and both -rem endings close their clause.

variations.cue: If you were learning the language, you should be reading the books.

variations.display: Sī linguam nōn discerem, librōs nōn legerem.
variations.cue: If I were not learning the language, I should not be reading the books.
If I learn the language, I shall read the books.
variations.changed: L1-M6's future in both halves, which claims it will happen

mistake.why: the second half left in the plain present. Both halves must be imagined — and this is the same slip as S03's on a longer sentence, which is where it actually happens: the further the second verb is from the first, the less an author remembers it belongs to the same mood.

sentences.usage: Said about a life you are not living.

sentences.display: Nisi aeger fuissem, ad scholam īssem.
sentences.cue: If I had not been ill, I would have gone to school.
sentences.literal: if-not ill I-had-been to school I-would-have-gone

words.note: 'If not, unless' — one word for two, and the fourth place in this course where a negative lives inside a word: nōlō, mālō, negō, nisi.
'Ill' — aeger, aegra, aegrum. L3-M7's word.
'I had been' — the pluperfect subjunctive of sum: fuī, fuisse, fuissem. L3-M10 wrote fuisse; this is the mood.
'To', with the object shape after it.
'School' after ad. L1-M6's word.
'I would have gone' — the pluperfect subjunctive of eō. The shortest verb in the course has a mood in every tense too.

sentences.trap: fuissem is the one a learner will use most, because most regrets are about a state rather than an act. L1-M5 gave you fuī, L3-M10 gave you fuisse, and this is the third shape of that stem — and the tense the whole course has done without is still not here: it is M8's.
sentences.sound: NI-si AE-ger fu-IS-sem, ad SCHO-lam ĪS-sem. Fourteen syllables and the two -issem endings rhyme across the comma.

variations.cue: If I had not been ill, I would have gone home.
variations.changed: L2-M4's home, which needs no ad

variations.display: Nisi aegra fuissem, ad scholam īssem.
variations.cue: If I had not been ill, I would have gone to school.
variations.changed: spoken by a woman, so the adjective moves

variations.display: Nisi aeger fuisset, ad scholam īsset.
variations.cue: If he had not been ill, he would have gone to school.

mistake.display: Nisi aeger eram, ad scholam īssem.
mistake.why: an INDICATIVE imperfect, which this course has never written. eram is still a free key after thirty-two modules and M8 of this level spends it — so the sentence reaches for a form the learner has not been given, in order to put the wrong mood in a counterfactual.

sentences.usage: Said accounting for a day you lost.
sentences.mnemonic: fuī, fuisse, fuissem — and eram is still to come.

sentences.display: Utinam linguam discerem; sī tempus habērem, discerem.
sentences.cue: If only I were learning the language; if I had time, I should be learning it.
sentences.literal: if-only language I-were-learning if time I-had I-should-learn

words.note: 'If only' — a particle for a wish, and with the pluperfect subjunctive it is a wish about the past, which is to say a regret.
'Language' as the thing learned. L3-M2's word.
'If only I were learning' — the imperfect subjunctive of discō. With utinam it is a wish about NOW rather than about the past.
'If'. L3-M4's word, and the mood after it decides everything: indicative for an open condition, subjunctive for one merely imagined.
'Time' — neuter, so it looks the same as a subject and as an object. English 'temporary' and 'tempo' come from it.
'If I had' — the imperfect subjunctive of habeō, denying the present. Its pluperfect habuissem denies the past instead.
'I should be learning' — the imperfect subjunctive of discō, and the SAME shape as its first appearance in this sentence. The frame around it decides whether it is a wish or a result.

sentences.trap: The same word twice with two jobs: after utinam it is a wish and after sī it is the result of a condition. One mood, one tense, one shape — and this is the module's whole argument, that Latin marks 'not real' once and lets the frame say what kind of unreality it is.
sentences.sound: U-ti-nam LIN-guam dis-CE-rem; SĪ TEM-pus ha-BĒ-rem, dis-CE-rem. Eighteen syllables and three -rem endings.

variations.display: Utinam linguam discerem; sī tempus habērem, legerem.
variations.cue: If only I were learning the language; if I had time, I should read.
If I had time, I should be learning the language.
variations.changed: the wish dropped, which leaves a plain condition

variations.cue: If only I had had time.
variations.changed: the past instead, so the tense moves to the pluperfect

mistake.display: Utinam linguam discerem; sī tempus habeō, discerem.
mistake.why: the condition left in the plain present while everything around it is imagined. sī tempus habeō would mean 'if I do have time', which contradicts the wish two words earlier — and a sentence that both wishes for something and asserts it is available says nothing at all.

sentences.usage: Said about a thing you keep meaning to do.
sentences.mnemonic: One mood marks 'not real'; the frame says what kind.

comprehensionPool.cue: If I had come, I would have seen.
If he were coming, I should be glad.
If you had not made a mistake, you would have come.
If only I had not made a mistake.

comprehensionPool.display: Sī hōrā sextā vēnissēs, medicum vīdissēs.
comprehensionPool.cue: If you had come at the sixth hour, you would have seen the doctor.
If you were learning the language, you should be reading the books.

comprehensionPool.display: Nisi aeger fuisset, ad scholam īsset.
comprehensionPool.cue: If he had not been ill, he would have gone to school.
If I had time, I should be learning the language.
If only I had had time.
I should like you to come.
